title: School Notebooks 5-pack

drivers.name: Promotion: 30% off
drivers.evidence: Past 10% off promotions lifted sales x1.11 on average, but this is a deeper 28% price drop. The product showed strong lift post-Easter (28 units) after a price increase, suggesting sensitivity. However, only one past promotion at this discount depth, so shrink toward 1.0. Noise-adjusted estimate: x1

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 10.2. A 30% discount on a 5-pack notebook is a deep price cut, but past promotions (10% off) only lifted sales 11% on average, and the noise-adjusted effect is x1.0. The classical model’s 1.00 suggestion reflects this weak signal. However, the price drop is 28% vs regular price—larger than any past promotion—and the product shows strong seasonal lift around back-to-school (last year's 10/20 promotion was in that season). Mother's Day (week before) reduced sales, suggesting demand is time-sensitive. The 2026-04-20 week (post-Easter) was weak (10 units), but the 2026-04-06 week (post-Easter) sold 28 units—likely due to a price increase. This week's price is now lower than ever. The baseline already reflects a 22.9% trend, so we adjust upward but modestly. Evidence is thin (1 past promotion at 30% off), so shrink toward 1.0. A moderate uplift is justified.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 10.2 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 22.0 | 10%-90%: 1.8 - 18.8

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-67% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
